planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall into moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; avoid waterlogged sites.

directions: A broad-leaved selection of greater woodrush with extra-wide, glossy, hair-fringed dark green leaves that often twist gently at the tip, giving a coarser, more textural clump than the species. Tasseled golden-brown flower spikes arch above the foliage from mid-spring into early summer. It spreads at a moderate pace into a dense, weed-suppressing evergreen mat well suited to difficult dry shade under trees, and tolerates heavier shade than most ornamental grasses. Rake out dead foliage in late winter and divide only when clumps become congested, since it resents frequent disturbance.

planting.note: Plant small divisions in spring into rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, shielding from hot reflected sun.

directions: This compact selection of hairy woodrush forms an unusually dense, bristly, hedgehog-like mound of narrow, glossy dark green evergreen leaves rather than the looser, sparser habit of the wild species. Its small scale and tidy mounding form suit rock gardens, shade container plantings, and the front edge of a woodland border where larger woodrush species would overwhelm neighbors. It needs steadier moisture than its tougher relatives, especially through summer heat, and resents prolonged drought or reflected heat from pavement. Comb out spent foliage in spring and avoid cutting it back hard in fall or winter, since the evergreen leaves provide its main seasonal interest.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in average, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; it tolerates more light than most woodrushes if soil stays evenly moist.

directions: A German-named selection of white woodrush (the name translates roughly as 'little snow rabbit'), grown for an especially heavy, fluffy show of small white-bracted flower clusters held above narrow, grass-like dark green leaves in late spring. It forms a tidy, clumping tuft rather than spreading aggressively, and the pale flower haze shows up well against darker woodland groundcovers and ferns. It adapts to sun or shade but colors and flowers most heavily with at least a few hours of direct light and consistent moisture. Comb out old foliage in early spring and divide clumps when flowering declines after several years.
